passages.title: Saving the Sydney Seahorse
passages.body:
Saving the Sydney Seahorse

Can Sydney seahorses born in aquariums¹ rescue their species from extinction?
Marine scientists are making desperate efforts to breed the Sydney seahorse in
aquariums because 90% of these creatures have disappeared over the past ten
[5] years. The scientists plan to set the seahorses free into the ocean after a short
period in the aquarium.

Also known as White's seahorse, the Sydney seahorse can grow up to 16
centimetres long and it lives on the east coast of Australia in shallow waters,
where its natural habitats are sponges, soft corals and seagrasses. However,
[10] due to a number of issues, such as adverse weather conditions, boat anchors
and declining water quality, this habitat is rapidly vanishing. In fact, vast numbers
of soft coral and sponge habitats have been lost over the past decade, at sites
where the seahorse was once common. This has caused a massive drop in
seahorse numbers and so seahorses are now classed as an endangered
[15] species. In an attempt to recover the dwindling seahorse numbers, a
conservation project has been launched which is described as a 'world first'.

Aquarium-bred babies

As part of the project, scientists took six pairs of adult seahorses from Sydney
harbour and brought them back to the aquarium tanks for breeding.

[20] 'Once they'd adapted to their new surroundings, the seahorses had many babies
and we are now rearing² these little ones,' says one of the senior scientists on
the project.

Unusually, it is the male seahorses that give birth to the tiny babies. They have
between 50 and 150 of them, and each one is only 1 cm long.

[25] 'In the ocean, baby seahorses are like sweeties – all sorts of animals enjoy
eating them,' laughs the scientist. 'In the aquarium, they're safe.'

Survival is not certain

Although the seahorses' chances of survival are significantly increased by
breeding in the aquarium, there is no guarantee they will adjust well to life in the
[30] wild.

'After these seahorses are freed from the aquarium tanks into the sea, there is
nobody to look after them or feed them each day. They will meet other animals
like fish and octopus which will prey on them. So, while we want to believe that
they will adapt to life in the wild, we cannot promise that they will survive out
[35] there.'

Hotels for seahorses

By the time the baby seahorses have grown to 4 cm in length, each one will be
tagged for identification and then released in one of two locations in Sydney
Harbour.

[40] These two locations are a natural and an artificial habitat. Surprisingly, it is shark
nets³ that are considered the natural habitat, and the artificial habitat is the
seahorse hotel that the scientists put in.

These seahorse hotels are cages made from wire. They were the original idea of
the senior scientist working on the project and are created to eventually look and
[45] feel like the seahorse habitats that are being threatened. Specialist divers can
check how well the shark nets and seahorse hotels are working underwater so
that the scientists can make a decision about whether to build more.

It is hoped that the seahorse hotels might provide homes for the wild seahorses
still living in the harbour. This should help the species to recover over time.

[50] The Sydney seahorse conservation project is likely to last for two years, or until
the scientists have an idea if it is actually helping this rare species.

Glossary

¹aquarium: a glass container of water where fish and other water creatures live
²rearing: bringing up and caring for young animals
³shark nets: underwater barriers to keep sharks out

items.stem:

items.stem:
Do you think this conservation project will be a success? Write Yes or No.

Give two reasons for your opinion. Support each reason with a quotation from the text.

Reason 1:
Quotation 1:
Reason 2:
Quotation 2:

accepted: making desperate efforts to breed the Sydney seahorse in aquariums because 90% of these creatures have disappeared over the past ten years
In the aquarium, they're safe
the seahorse hotels might provide homes for the wild seahorses
They will meet other animals like fish and octopus which will prey on them
we cannot promise that they will survive out there
there is nobody to look after them or feed them each day
divers can check how well the shark nets and seahorse hotels are working underwater
there is no guarantee they will adjust well to life in the wild

items.note: A person must mark this: 1 mark for each appropriate reason (max 2) and 1 mark for each matching quotation (max 2). Yes: removed from danger/kept in a tank ('making desperate efforts to breed… over the past ten years'); safe as babies ('In the aquarium, they're safe.'); hotels for safety ('the seahorse hotels might provide homes for the wild seahorses'). No: still have predators ('They will meet other animals like fish and octopus which will prey on them.'); used to being safe and fed / might not adapt ('we cannot promise that they will survive out there.' / 'there is nobody to look after them or feed them each day.'); might not use the hotels ('divers can check how well the shark nets and seahorse hotels are working underwater'); might not adapt to sea water ('there is no guarantee they will adjust well to life in the wild.'). Accept any other appropriate reason supported by a matching quotation.

items.stem:
Write an article for your school website about how you could encourage local species of insects, birds or any other animals in your area.

This might be in your garden, on a balcony, in the school grounds, a nearby park or other outdoor space.

Think about:
• what habitat they live in
• what food they eat
• what you can do to protect them.

Plan your article first, then write it.
items.note: Marked with the Stage 5 writing rubric: Creation of texts 5, Vocabulary and language 3, Grammar and punctuation 7, Structure of texts 7, Word structure (spelling) 3. 0 marks for 20 words or fewer; maximum 7 marks for 21–60 words.
